reasoning: Recent public polling and forecasting still show Republican Sen. Tom Cotton with a very large advantage over Democrat Hallie Shoffner in Arkansas, with the only quantified polling average in the last few months around an R+18–22 margin and prediction markets heavily favoring a Republican hold.[1][2][4] Given Arkansas’s strong R+15 Cook PVI and the absence of newer contradictory polls within the last 45 days, the current evidence supports an Arkansas Senate race environment of roughly **R+20** and a clearly Republican-favored outcome.[1][2][4]

sources.name: Prediction Edge (poll aggregation from FiftyPlusOne / GrayHouse)
sources.details: GrayHouse/FiftyPlusOne Arkansas Senate poll and aggregate show Tom Cotton leading Hallie Shoffner 58% to 36%, an R+22 margin, with a polling average of Cotton+22 updated June 30, 2026.

sources.name: PollsMax (GrayHouse poll average)
sources.details: PollsMax Arkansas Senate polling average, based on one GrayHouse poll, shows 56.0% R to 38.0% D, an R+18 margin between Cotton and Shoffner.

sources.name: Prediction Edge – Arkansas Senate winner by party (prediction market)
sources.details: PredictionEdge "Arkansas Senate winner by party" market gives Republicans about 97% and Democrats about 5% implied odds, indicating a strongly Republican-favored race (effectively R+20+ environment rather than a close contest).
sources.date_range: Market odds live as of late July–early August 2026

sources.name: Cook Political Report – Partisan Voting Index (Arkansas statewide)
sources.details: Cook Partisan Voting Index rates Arkansas at R+15 statewide, indicating the state votes about 15 points more Republican than the national average in recent presidential elections.
sources.date_range: Structural index, no specific date range (Cook PVI baseline)

sources.name: Arkansas Times
sources.details: Arkansas Times feature on Hallie Shoffner’s campaign describes the race as an uphill battle in a heavily Republican state, characterizing Cotton as a strong favorite without presenting contrary polling closer than the existing R+18–22 numbers.
